headline: High risk of data leakage and cascading errors: oh-my-openagent’s broad network/tooling can expose context while interacting with a non-runnable content-writing peer.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no documented shared channel, but B uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and can ingest files and messages; if A’s content is copied into B’s workspace or prompts, B may treat it as trusted instructions. Because A is a content-writing agent and B can run browsers/subprocesses, the interaction pathway is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF A’s output is pasted into B’s prompt or AGENTS.md
IF B reads A-generated files from a shared workspace without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of A outputs into B prompts
Require provenance tags on any A-generated file
Use a separate workspace per agent
Add a manual review step before B executes instructions from A
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization on shared channels

B_data_leakage.rationale: B explicitly touches project code, AGENTS.md, README.md, session history, and provider auth data, and has broad network egress; A is a content-writing agent with broad egress. If they share a workspace or credentials, B can leak A-associated content or secrets to third-party services. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF A and B share the same filesystem or repo checkout
IF B is configured to upload file contents or session history to external APIs
mitigations: Separate credentials and workspaces
Turn off external API calls for sensitive projects
Restrict B to a read-only clone
Clear session history before switching agents
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B can spawn subprocesses and supports multiple instances with per-installation session scope, while A’s profile exposes broad network egress. If both operate on the same mutable project or installation state, they can race on files, configs, or network-backed resources. The profiles do not show locking or isolation between them, so conflict is plausible in default multi-agent use.
conditions: IF A and B write to the same repository or config directory
IF B runs multiple instances against the same installation
mitigations: Run only one writer at a time
Use separate clones per agent
Lock shared config files during edits
Disable subprocess spawning for shared-state tasks
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: B’s support-oriented toolchain can act on upstream content, and A is a content-writing agent whose outputs may be treated as authoritative text. If B consumes A’s generated prose or instructions without verification, errors can cascade into browser actions, messages, or code edits. The pathway is inferred, not directly documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text as source material without review
IF B sends messages or edits code based on A’s output
mitigations: Require human review of A outputs before action
Ask B to cite source lines before acting
Limit B to drafting-only mode
Add a verification checklist for downstream actions
requires-engineering: implement confidence gating on A-to-B handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles provider authentication data, installation identifiers, and session history, while A has broad network egress. If regulated or sensitive data is routed through B and then out through A-associated workflows, retention and residency obligations can diverge. No specific jurisdiction mismatch is documented, so this is a general compliance-risk medium finding rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed in B’s session history or auth prompts
IF A-associated workflows transmit that data to external services
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data through either agent
Purge session history after each task
Use separate accounts for sensitive and non-sensitive work
Review retention settings for external APIs
requires-engineering: document residency and retention boundaries per agent
